paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.71:1 Rule 3.71 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.71. 1. Applicable principles where causes of action misjoined On the authorities, the principles which should be considered in determining whether the joinder of defendants in one action is appropriate are these: (1) Whether the claims of the plaintiff arise out of the same transaction or series of transactions… (2) Whether or not there is a common issue of law or fact of sufficient importance to render it desirable that the claims against the proposed defendant be tried together. (3) Whether the expense and delay that would be caused by compelling the plaintiff to bring separate actions against the proposed defendant would be greatly out of proportion to the inconvenience, expense or embarrassment which that defendant would be put if the actions were tried together. (4) … if the liability of the proposed defendant is contingent upon the plaintiff first establishing that he suffered a loss in respect of the transaction with the named defendant, then the application to join the proposed defendant may be considered premature. In my view, where the alternative claims arise out of the same transaction or series of transactions and involve a common question of fact or law, then the governing principle in determining whether joinder should be allowed is the third principle set out above, namely, the balance of convenience. The fact that the alternative claim against the defendants may be unnecessary, if the plaintiff succeeds against the main defendants, is only one consideration to be weighed and should not, by itself, be considered a conclusive reason for refusing the joinder. Thames Steel Construction v. Portman (1980), 111 D.L.R. (3d) 460 at 467-68 (Ont. Div. Ct.). 2. Discretion of Court The matter of whether a counterclaim should be ordered to be tried separately is a matter of judicial discretion and accordingly a consideration of previous decisions is of limited assistance … if the only connection between a claim and a counterclaim is that the parties are the same, an application to have the counterclaim tried separately is likely to be successful … … in exercising the discretion of the court in this matter one must be mindful of the provision of sec. 8 of the Judicature Act, R.S.A. 1980, ch. J-1 that all multiplicity of legal proceedings be avoided … A number of the cases cited by counsel involved situations where a defendant had counterclaimed and added as a party defendant to the counterclaim a party not previously joined in the proceedings. The cases indicate that such a counterclaim should not be struck out or ordered to be tried separately as long as the relief claimed in such counterclaim is relating to or connected with the original subject of the cause or matter, although there must be something more than a mere factual connection. The concept was succinctly stated by Orde, J.A., in Export Brewing and Malting Co. v. Dominion Bank, [1932] O.R. 446 … as follows at page 449: When, as here, the defendant by his counterclaim seeks some relief against the plaintiff with others not already parties to the action, it becomes necessary to determine whether or not the plaintiff is properly a party to the cross action which the defendant desires to engraft upon the plaintiff's action. If he is not, then it is clear that the counterclaim is embarassing to the plaintiff, because if he is not concerned with the subject matter of the defendant's claims for relief, he ought not to have the proceedings in his action clogged by proceeding against strangers. Mosychuk v. Gunderson (1983), 45 A.R. 145 at 147-48 (Master). 3. Test An order under R. 95 effectively relegates a counterclaim to a true cross-action, that is, a separate action by the defendant which is to proceed separately from the plaintiff's action. One of the purposes, if not the purpose, of counterclaims is to avoid multiplicity of proceedings. An order under R. 95 causes multiplicity of proceedings. Rule 95 itself recognizes, in its test, that multiplicity is to be avoided unless it is necessary to any particular action. The rule dictates when it is necessary to have effectively separate actions. The sole test in an application under R. 95 is whether the counterclaim can be conveniently disposed of in the same action. If it cannot, the court may grant an appropriate order. It is not a ground for an order under R. 95 that the counterclaim is for a lesser amount than the plaintiff's claim. If it were so all counterclaims, except those where the amount claimed equals or exceeds the plaintiff's claim, would be relegated to separate cross-actions … The “convenience” is in reference to having the counterclaim disposed of in the same action. That is the test enunciated in Kaps Transport Ltd. v. McGregor Telephone & Power Construction Co. (1970), 73 W.W.R. (N.S.) 549 (C.A.). Bank of British Columbia v. Affkor Group Ltd. (1983), 21 Alta. L.R. 377 at 380-81 (Master).

paragraphs.heading: Part 3. Court Actions

sentences.text: Consolidation or separation of claims and actions

paragraphs.text: (1) The Court may order one or more of the following: (a) that 2 or more claims or actions be consolidated; (b) that 2 or more claims or actions be tried at the same time or one after the other; (c) that one or more claims or actions be stayed until another claim or action is determined; (d) that a claim be asserted as a counterclaim in another action. (2) An order under subrule (1) may be made for any reason the Court considers appropriate, including, without limitation, that 2 or more claims or actions (a) have a common question of law or fact, or (b) arise out of the same transaction or occurrence or series of transactions or occurrences.

(d) that a claim be asserted as a counterclaim in another action.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.72:1 Rule 3.72 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.72. 1. General Rule for Joinder In Klychak v. Samchuk, 2012 ABQB 85, 2012 CarswellAlta 118, 532 A.R. 259; additional reasons 2012 ABQB 314, 2012 CarswellAlta 867, Justice Veit said, at paragraphs 38-39: 38 Rules 3.72 and 1.4(1) and s. 8 of the Judicature Act outline the Court's authority to order actions to be tried at the same time or one after the other. Case law, including Valerio and Mikisew, outline the types of factors which a court should consider when deciding whether to exercise its power under the Rules and the statute; although individual factors should be considered, the court's overall objective is to ensure that its decision on how the actions should be tried will serve the ends of justice: Alliance Pipeline. 39 Much of the case law cited by the parties was developed under the former Rules of Court; because of the similarity between the old Rules and the current ones, the existing case law continues to be applicable. Indeed, Rule 1.4 emphasizes the need to foster just and fair resolutions of disputes in a timely and cost-effective way. In Munro v. Munro, 2011 ABCA 279, 2011 CarswellAlta 1670, 50 Alta. L.R. (5th) 247, 50 Alta. L.R. (5th) 421, 2 R.F.L. (7th) 298, 341 D.L.R. (4th) 635, 513 A.R. 363, 530 W.A.C. 363, the husband appealed the dismissal of his application for an order to consolidate an action for breach of a matrimonial property agreement and an application for retroactive child support. At paragraphs 6-7, Justices Paperny and Bielby said: 6 An order to consolidate is discretionary, and the standard of review is reasonableness: Alliance Pipeline Limited v. Universal Ensco, Inc, 2007 ABCA 285 at para. 3; 417 AR 1. Absent a material error in principle, a significant misapprehension or disregard of the evidence, or a decision which is clearly wrong, an appellate court will not interfere with an exercise of discretion: AB v. CD, 2008 ABCA 51 at para. 10; 85 Alta LR (4th) 18. 7 When faced with an application to consolidate claims, a court must weigh several relevant factors. They include the extent to which there are common claims and disputes, and the possibility that consolidation may save time and resources in pre-trial procedures and at trial. The court must also consider potential prejudice to the parties which may arise from consolidation if, for example, one action is more advanced than the other and if consolidation will result in prejudicial delay of a trial. Master Smart, in Wong v. Leung, 2011 ABQB 722, 2011 CarswellAlta 2052, 530 A.R. 91 (Master), adopted that test (at paragraph 24). See also: AutoCanada Capital Motors GP Inc v. Mirbach, 2021 ABQB 170, 2021 CarswellAlta 474 at para. 6. In Center Street Limited Partnership v. Lloyd's Underwriters, 2017 ABQB 295, 2017 CarswellAlta 734, 50 Alta. L.R. (6th) 217 (Master), Master Robertson said: 12 The guiding principles in considering whether two or more cases should be consolidated or tried together were set out succinctly by the Court of Appeal in Alliance Pipeline Limited v C.E. Franklin Ltd, 2007 ABCA 285 at para. 6: The purpose of consolidation is to enhance the administration of justice. A court should consider the possibility of inconsistent verdicts, the prospect of prejudice to the parties and the impact of consolidation and non-consolidation, both at the pre-trial and trial stages on scarce resources, including administrative, judicial and financial. In other words, a court must be able to conclude that having regard to all the circumstances, on balance, it is in the interests of justice that the actions be consolidated. Some of the relevant factors that should be considered are discussed in Mikisew[cited below]. These, however, are not necessarily the only relevant factors, nor are they in themselves determinative. Each case must be assessed on its own merits and should include consideration, not just of the common claims, but the extent of the distinct claims between the parties. The focus in each case must be on the impact of consolidation on the parties and on the administration of justice. See also Anokhina v. Banovic, 2019 ABQB 774, 2019 CarswellAlta 2093 (paragraphs 20–23) for a summary of the law by Justice Lema. The following cases were decided under the previous Rules: Broadly speaking, where claims by or against different parties involve or may involve a common question of law or fact bearing sufficient importance in proportion to the rest of the action to render it desirable that the whole of the matters should be disposed of at the same time the Court will allow the joinder of plaintiffs or defendants, subject to its discretion as to how the action should be tried. Edmonton (City) v. Dominion Stores Ltd. (1960), 23 D.L.R. (2d) 677 (Alta. C.A.), at 680, per Ford C.J.A., quoting with approval Payne v. British Time Recorder Co., [1921] 2 K.B. 1 at 16. 2. When to Apply An application to split the action should be left to the trial judge. We have in the instant case a common question or questions of law in the different causes of action alleged against the different defendants, and this question, or questions as they may be, are fundamental to the success or failure of the entire action. True, the law may not be applicable in the same way to the different facts alleged in respect of each transaction, but that is for the trial Judge to decide …Edmonton (City) v. Dominion Stores Ltd. (1960), 23 D.L.R. (2d) 677 at 681 (Alta. C.A.). 3. Generally The general principle relating to the granting of a consolidation order is that the issues in both actions are identical… The underlying principle of R. 229 is to prevent the waste of resources by needless litigation. Welco Expediting Ltd. v. Harris (1995), 31 Alta. L.R. (3d) 173 (Q.B.), at 187, per Moshansky J. And Medhurst J. said: There is provision in R. 229 of the Rules of Court for the consolidation of actions that (a) have a common question of law or fact, or (b) arise out of the same transaction or series of transactions. (See also R. 36 re joinder of causes of action). It is also stated in s. 32(k) [am. 1978, c. 51, s. 28] of the Judicature Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 193 that “as far as possible all matters in controversy between the parties [can] be completely determined and all multiplicity of legal proceedings concerning any such matters avoided.” The effect of consolidation is to combine two or more actions so that thereafter they will proceed as one action. One of the principal purposes of consolidation is to save expense and to avoid multiplicity of pleadings and proceedings. In Flitney v. Howard, [1958] O.R. 701 (C.A.), Morden J.A. observed that this purpose would only be accomplished if such an order were made at a very early stage and it would not be accomplished if granted on the eve of the trial. Scheidl v. Southam Inc. (1981), 16 Alta. L.R. (2d) 158 at 161 (Q.B.). This decision was reversed in result by the Court of Appeal [unreported] but the proposition was not criticized. See Hagman v. Omar Holdings Ltd. (1984), 55 A.R. 44 (Master), at 45, for a note of the appeal proceedings. In Hagman v. Omar Holdings Ltd. Master Funduk continued: 5. Rule 229 is not restricted to situations falling within items (a) or (b). There is a third catch all category, being “where for any other reason it is desirable to make an order under this Rule”. In Norwester Ltd. v. British Aviation Insurance Company Limited, 4 Alta. L.R. (2d) 133 (N.W.T.S.C.), Tallis, J., indicates that there are two types of orders than can be granted at the same time, being an order that the actions be consolidated and an order that the actions be tried together. He indicates that in the second case that: 2. The actions may be ordered to be tried together. They are then set down on the list one after the other to be tried in such manner as the court directs. The trial judge has a discretion to direct that the evidence in one action is to be taken as evidence in the other action or actions. Nevertheless the actions maintain their separate identity and there are separate pleadings, discoveries, judgments and bills of costs. If the actions are tried together they are tried concurrently. In my view there is a third type of order, being that the actions be tried one after the other. In that case the actions are tried consecutively. In Giberson v. Labatt Breweries of British Columbia, [1980] 1 W.W.R. 93, (B.C. S.C.), Legg, J., ordered two actions to be tried at the same time. He states, at p. 96: In the case at bar it is apparent from the pleadings that all the facts and circumstances giving rise to the event which caused the plaintiff's injury will be canvassed before the trial judge in the first action. It therefore appears reasonable that the same trial judge should determine the question of whether the defendant solicitors are liable in the second action at the same time. It is submitted, however, that the defendant solicitors should not be put to the inconvenience and expense of attending at the trial of the first action if a consolidation is ordered or of awaiting the outcome of the first action if it is ordered that the two actions be tried at the same time or on the same day. Against this there is the convenience of the plaintiff in seeking to have all her causes of action arising out of the circumstances which gave rise to both actions adjudicated by the same trial judge and, if possible, on the same general occasion of trial. On appeal, reported, [1980] 2 W.W.R. 689 (C.A.), was dismissed. McFarlane, J.A., for the court, states at p. 689: I point out that the trial judge did not order these actions consolidated; neither did he unequivocally direct that they be tried at the same time, in the sense that all of the evidence in the one case would be evidence in the other. His reasons for judgment, the effect of which is carried into the formal order, provide that the two actions be tried at the same time or on the same day and with all subject to the discretion of the trial judge. I think the possible objections which have been raised as grounds of appeal are matters properly to be taken into consideration by the judge before whom these two actions come to be tried, and I see no basis upon which this court would be justified in allowing the appeal. Hagman v. Omar Holdings Ltd. (1984), 55 A.R. 44 at 46-47 (Master). Hagman v. Omar Holdings Ltd. was approved in Henuset Brothers Ltd. v. I.U.O.E., Local 955 (1984), 57 A.R. 258 at 265 (Q.B.). Moore C.J.Q.B., in Northland Bank v. Willson (1997), 56 Alta. L.R. (3d) 130 (Q.B.), at p. 135, said the following about the purpose of the rule: In Reichmann v. Toronto Life Publishing Co. (No. 1) (1988), 31 C.P.C. (2d) 54 (Ont. S.C.), the court held that the overriding purpose of the rules consolidating matters is to secure the just determination of the matters in dispute by assessing the balance of convenience to the plaintiffs and defendants. Moore J., in Mikisew Cree First Nation v. Canada (1998), 224 A.R. 157 (Q.B.), set forth factors that should be considered in an application to consolidate actions. At p. 158, His Lordship said: In Shah v. Bakkenn (1996), 46 C.P.C. (3d) 205 (B.C. C.A.) (sic; the Shah decision was a decision of Master Joyce of the B.C.S.C.), the court lists a number of factors which [one] should take into account in an application to consolidate. These include: i) whether there are common claims, disputes and relationships between the parties; ii) whether consolidation will save time and resources in pretrial procedures; iii) whether time at trial will be reduced; iv) whether one party will be seriously prejudiced by having two trials together; v) whether one action is at a more advanced stage than the other; and vi) whether consolidation will delay the trial of one action which will cause serious prejudice to one party. Kent J., in Andy & Jean Grebely Holdings Ltd. v. Commercial Union Assurance Co. of Canada, 2000 ABQB 604, 2000 CarswellAlta 958, (sub nom. Grebely v. Economical Mutual Insurance Co., 282 A.R. 296, agreed that the above noted factors are the ones to be considered in an old rule 229 (current rule 3.72) application (see p. 299). Justice Kenny, in Frydman v. Pelletier, 2013 ABQB 225, 2013 CarswellAlta 495, 559 A.R. 388, said, at paragraph 40: 40 The court maintains discretion as to when it is appropriate to consolidate actions under Rule 3.72. Some factors to consider are set out in Mikisew Cree First Nation v. Canada (1998), 224 AR 157 (QB) at p 158. These are: a) whether there are common claims, disputes, and relationships between the parties; b) whether consolidation will save time and resources in pretrial procedures; c) whether time at trial will be reduced; d) whether one party will be seriously prejudiced by having two trials together; e) whether one action is at a more advanced stage than the other; and f) whether consolidation will delay the trial of one action which will cause serious prejudice to one party. 4. Onus In Meyer v. Altex Energy Ltd., 2019 ABQB 787, 2019 CarswellAlta 2365, Justice Woolley discussed the onus borne by the party seeking consolidation of actions: [15] I also reject the Respondents' position that the Applicants bear a “heavy onus” in relation to consolidation. The Respondents cite jurisprudence from the Federal Court which states that the onus is on the party seeking consolidation to prove that the respondent parties would not suffer applicable prejudice or injustice: Sanofi-Aventis Canada Inc v Novopharm Ltd 2009 FC 1285 at para 11. In some cases the Federal Court has described this as a “heavy onus”: Mon-Oil Ltd v R (1989) 47 FTR 50 cited in Sanofi-Aventis at para 12. [16] I agree that the Applicants bear the onus of showing that consolidation is appropriate. But that onus is not “heavy.” It is neither heavy nor light; it is simply an onus to show on the balance of probabilities that this matter is an appropriate one for consolidation in accordance with Rule 3.72 and the governing jurisprudence. I note in this respect that the test for consolidation concerns the administration of justice and conserving judicial resources and, significantly, that wasting judicial resources puts access to justice at risk. The interests at stake in a consolidation application are not merely those of the parties, but take into account the broader community who seek access to the court system. As a judge of this court I am obligated to protect the administration of justice and to ensure the proper use of judicial and other resources, and my consideration of those matters ought not to be limited through imposing an unusual or undue onus on an applicant. 5. Order Should Not Be Granted if it Will Delay Litigation In Ellis-Don Management Services v. Rae-Dawn Construction Ltd. (1992), 131 A.R. 190 (C.A.), the court considered an order which directed that certain construction lawsuits could not be tried until judgment was rendered in related insurance proceedings. The construction lawsuits were advancing at a slower pace than the other matters. The Court of Appeal, speaking through Côté J.A., set aside the order and, at p. 191, said: It is desirable to try to do something to avoid duplication of proceedings or inconsistent verdicts. But in our view that cannot always be done, and should not be done where it unfairly retards litigation. 6. Consolidation versus Trials at Same Time In my view the allegations in these two actions fall squarely within the requirements of Rule 229. However, I do not think it is in the best interests of the parties that the two actions be consolidated for trial for, as I understand the effect of this type of order, it would make one action out of the two and create a great deal of confusion as to who are plaintiffs, defendants and plaintiffs and defendants by counterclaim. Rule 229 also provides that the court can order that the actions be tried at the same time and this seems to me to be far less cumbersome while achieving the desirable result of allowing a Trial Judge to hear all of the relevant matters without the necessity of two separate trials covering similar evidence and witnesses. Athabasca Realty Co. v. Humeniuk (1978), 14 A.R. 79 (T.D.), at 85, per Miller J. And Medhurst J. said: The alternate question to consider, however, is whether the two actions should be tried at the same time, as directed by the master. This is the order that is usually made when consolidation orders cannot for some reason be granted inasmuch as the avoidance of additional expense and multiplicity of actions can usually be accomplished in this way. Provision for such an order is set out in R. 229 and the same factors need to be considered as in an application for a consolidation order. Scheidl v. Southam Inc. (1981), 16 Alta. L.R. (2d) 158 (Q.B.), (reversed in result by C.A., but the proposition was not criticized, see Hagman v. Omar Holdings Ltd., supra, at 45). 7. Stay of Proceedings In Jardine Lloyd Thompson Canada Inc. v. Western Oil Sands Inc., 2006 ABQB 933, 2006 CarswellAlta 1750, 406 A.R. 23, 67 Alta. L.R. (4th) 165, Wittmann A.C.J.Q.B. had before him an application for a stay of proceedings “pending the outcome of related arbitration proceedings.” His Lordship reviewed the law, and concluded that he was bound by principles set forth in Alberta v. A.U.P.E. (1984), 53 A.R. 277 (Alta. C.A.), but that they are to be applied in a manner consistent with the efficient resolution of the disputes. He specifically found such an approach to be preferable to the stricter approach taken by Master Funduk in Bank of British Columbia v. Sitko (1986), 68 A.R. 65 (Alta. Q.B.). A.C.J. Wittmann said, at pp. 168–170: 9 The parties are agreed that this Court has jurisdiction to grant a stay of proceedings, that the remedy is discretionary and that it must be exercised in accordance with established principles. Those principles were described by Belzil J.A. in Alberta, Province of v. Alberta, Union Provincial Employees (1984), 53 A.R. 277 (C.A.) (“AUPE”), at paras. 9-10: The first and basic question to be addressed in such cases is whether the issues in the action sought to be stayed are substantially the same as those in the ‘test action’. If they are not, a stay will not be ordered … If the issues are substantially the same, a stay may and should be ordered if other tests are satisfied. Having thus concluded that the issues in the two proceedings are substantially the same, the remaining principles to be considered in determining whether this was a proper case for a stay are those set out by Scott, L.J., in St. Pierre v. South American Stores Ltd., [1935] All E.R. 408 (C.A.), at p.414:(I) a mere balance of convenience is not a sufficient ground for depriving a plaintiff of the advantages of prosecuting his action in English Court if it is otherwise properly brought. The right of access to the King's Court must not be lightly refused; (ii) in order to justify a stay two conditions must be satisfied, one positive and the other negative; (a) the defendant must satisfy the court that the continuance of the action would work an injustice because it would be oppressive, or vexatious to him, or would be an abuse of the powers of the court in some other way, and (b) the stay must not cause an injustice to the plaintiff. On both the burden of proof is on the defendant. 10 In Bank of British Columbia v. Sitko (1986), 68 A.R. 65 (Q.B.), Master Funduk considered AUPE and held, at paras.38-39: If an adjudication in the first action does not necessarily dispose of the issues in the second action it cannot be said there is a true duplication of proceedings in all respects. What is mandatory is that the issues be the same in both actions and that an adjudication in one action regardless of what that adjudication is, automatically disposes of the issues in the second action. 11 Consequently, Master Funduk was of the view that claims pleaded in the alternative are not appropriate for a stay. 12 A different approach was taken by the Ontario High Court in Boart Sweden Ab v. Nya Stromnes Ab., [1988] O.J. No. 2839 (H.C.). Boart concerned an action for breach of contract, as well as conspiracy to induce breach of contract and unlawful interference with economic relations arising out of the alleged breach of an exclusive distribution agreement. The parties to the agreement were bound by an arbitration clause, but the Ontario action added parties and causes of action that did not strictly arise out of the agreement itself. Campbell J. did not apply the test set out in AUPE. In fact, he cited no authority directly on the point but concluded at paras. 20-22 that it was appropriate to grant the stay. He said: The factual basis of all the issues in the Ontario action has to do with the conduct of the parties under the international agreement which is the subject of arbitration. To the extent that Boart Canada is an assignee of the rights of Boart Sweden under the international agreement it is bound by the arbitration agreement. It would be idle to proceed with the tort claims in Canada at the very same time that the arbitration proceeds in Sweden, even though the causes of action and the parties are not identical, when the factual basis of the tort claims is so tied up together with the matters being decided in the arbitration and when there is an obvious overlap between the witnesses required for the different proceedings in the two different countries. Campbell J. further noted, at para. 28: The matters in dispute in the Ontario action are inextricably bound up with the matter which the parties agreed to arbitrate. paragraphs.text: (1) No claim or action fails solely because (a) 2 or more parties join in an action that they should not have joined, (b) 2 or more parties do not join an action that they could or should have joined, or (c) a party was incorrectly named as a party or was incorrectly omitted from being named as a party. paragraphs.heading: Part 3. Court Actions

sentences.text: Adding, removing or substituting parties after close of pleadings

paragraphs.text: (1) After close of pleadings, no person may be added, removed or substituted as a party to an action started by statement of claim except in accordance with this rule. (2) On application, the Court may order that a person be added, removed or substituted as a party to an action if (a) in the case of a person to be added or substituted as plaintiff, plaintiff-by-counterclaim or third party plaintiff, the application is made by a person or party and the consent of the person proposed to be added or substituted as a party is filed with the application; (b) in the case of an application to add or substitute any other party, or to remove or to correct the name of a party, the application is made by a person or party and the Court is satisfied the order should be made. (3) The Court may not make an order under this rule if prejudice would result for a party that could not be remedied by a costs award, an adjournment or the imposition of terms. Alta. paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.74:1 Rule 3.74 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.74. 1. Overview In Manson Insulation Products Ltd. v. Crossroads C & I Distributors, 2011 ABQB 51, 2011 CarswellAlta 108, Poelman, J. said “Rule 3.74 governs amendments that add parties”: paragraph 47. His Lordship went on to say (at paragraphs 48–52): 48 The material parts for this application, where there is no consent, are rules 3.74(2)(b) and 3.74(3). These establish three requirements: a) the application must be made by a party; b) the court must be satisfied that an order should be made; and c) there must be no prejudice that could not be remedied. 49 The amendment application is made by New Manson, a party to both the claim and counterclaim. Thus, the first requirement is satisfied. 50 The rule gives no express guidance on what is meant by the second requirement, that the court be satisfied. It clearly intends to confer discretion on the court. Discretionary powers of the court must, of course, be exercised judicially—that is, in accordance with accepted principles. 51 In my view, for the reasons given above, the guidelines established by the authorities under the former rules should again inform the court's discretion under rule 3.74(2)(b). There is, therefore, no reason to take a different approach in principle to amendments that add parties, subject of course to the express inclusion of prejudice considerations in rule 3.74(3). 52 The third element, prejudice, is a consideration in any amendment application, according to the authorities. It is given more prominence where new parties are added, presumably because they are more likely to expand the scope and expense of an action, and may be particularly be affected where the action is well advanced or limitation periods have passed. In Hartwell v. Taylor, 2016 ABQB 289, 2016 CarswellAlta 952, at paragraph 14, Justice E. Wilson agreed with the above quote from Manson Insulation Products Ltd. v. Crossroads C & I Distributors, 2011 ABQB 51, 2011 CarswellAlta 108. In 869120 Alberta Ltd. v. B & G Energy Ltd., 2011 ABQB 209, 2011 CarswellAlta 512, [2011] A.J. No. 366, Justice Eidsvik discussed the test found in R. 3.74(2)(b). At paragraphs 22-24, her Ladyship said: 22 The test found in 3.74 (2) (b) states that the Court may order that a person be added if it is “satisfied that the order should be made”. Subsection 3 goes on to add however that “The Court may not make an order under this rule if prejudice would result for a party that could not be remedied by a costs award, an adjournment or the imposition of terms.” 23 The former Rules, rules 132 and 133, although somewhat differently worded, were similarly broad. The parties agreed that these new rules do not materially alter the legal test and accordingly reliance can be made on the case law on point to date. Indeed, subsection 3 basically codifies the “classic rule” that “an amendment should be allowed no matter how careless or late, unless there is prejudice” as outlined by Justice Côté in Balm v. 3512061 Canada Ltd. 2003 ABCA 98 at para. 43 and Milfive Inv. v. Sefel (1998) 216 A.R. 196. 24 The other criteria that is generally accepted is that the amendment must raise a triable issue, or otherwise said, not be “hopeless” (Stolk v. 382779 Alberta Inc. 2005 ABQB 440, Marin v. Rask 2000 ABQB 931), there must be a “modest degree of evidence” if the amendment is beyond trivial or of a clarifying nature, unless the claim to be added is fraud, and there a “stiffer test” is to be used (Balm at paras. 29 and 63). Finally, if the claim against a person to be added, or the cause of action is outside of the limitation period then reference is to be made to section 6 of the Limitation Act R.S.A. 2000 c. L-12 to determine if it should be allowed. In Saskatchewan Power Corporation v. Morgan Stanley Capital Group Inc., 2013 ABCA 341, 2013 CarswellAlta 1866, the Court discussed the law governing the adding of a party to litigation, and in particular, the adding of parties to leave to appeal applications. At paragraphs 1-2, and 7–12, Madam Justice C.D. Hunt said: 1 C.D. HUNT J.A.:—Morgan Stanley Capital Corp Inc. (Morgan Stanley) applies to be added as a respondent to four leave to appeal applications that will be heard by this Court on November 19, 2013. 2 Its applications are dismissed. If leave to appeal is granted, it can re-apply for party or intervener status. … 7 The parties share a common view about the test for adding a party to litigation. An applicant must show a legal interest in the outcome of the proceeding; its inclusion is just and convenient; and its interests will only be adequately protected if it is granted status: Carbon Development Partnership v. Alberta (Energy Utilities Board), 2007 ABCA 231 at para 9 (available on CanLii) [Carbon]. 8 Only in exceptional circumstances should a party be granted respondent status prior to the decision in a leave application: Provident Energy Ltd. v. Alberta (Utilities Commission), 2008 ABCA 316 at para 8 (available on CanLii) [Provident]. The reason for this is obvious. Before a leave application is decided, it is impossible to predict if leave will be granted or in relation to what questions. 9 In these matters, leave can only be granted for questions of law or jurisdiction: Alberta Utilities Commission Act, SA 2007, c A-37.2, s 29(1). The test for leave to appeal requires the applicant to demonstrate that the question of law or jurisdiction raises a “serious, arguable point”: Provident at para 11. Subsumed in the general test are four elements: is the point on appeal of significance to the practice; is the point raised of significance to the action itself; is the appeal prima facie meritorious; and will the appeal unduly hinder the progress of the action. 10 If leave to appeal is granted, a party can then apply to participate in the appeal as a respondent or an intervener. At that stage the Court can better determine if and how the party's interests may be affected, and what if anything it may usefully contribute to the proceedings. 11 In applications for intervener status in a pending leave application, I was hesitant about granting their applications, but I did so because another party had already been granted intervener status and I was persuaded the applicants could assist the Court in deciding the leave application: Carbon at para 14. 12 I have considered TransCanada Pipeline Ventures Ltd v. Alberta Utilities Commission, 2009 ABCA 255, 460 AR 220 [TransCanada], where Justice O'Brien granted party status to Suncor in a pending leave application. He stressed, however, that Suncor was a true party, in contrast to the Commission itself which, as he said, should not be left to wholly defend its decision: TransCanada at para 10. In Lil Dude Ranch Ltd. v. 1229122 Alberta Inc., 2014 ABQB 39, 2014 CarswellAlta 82, 5 Alta. L.R. (6th) 154 (Master), Master Robertson said, at paragraph 23: 23 It is apparent that this rule is directed at making sure that a person added to an existing pleading in a plaintiff-type role is consenting to being added. It is easily read in conjunction with rule 3.56(1) in that there may be several defendants, but only one has counterclaimed, and later on an application is made for another defendant to join the counterclaim as plaintiff-by-counterclaim. This rule simply says that the new plaintiff-by-counterclaim must consent to the amendment. In 513320 Alberta Inc. v. Jean, 2015 ABQB 826, Justice Goss gave this overview: 24 Rule 3.62(1)(b) of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 2010/124 (“Rules”), allows a party to amend the party's pleading after the pleadings have closed in accordance with r 3.74 (adding, removing, substituting or correcting the name of a party) and r 3.65 (all other amendments). Rule 3.74 requires the Court to be satisfied that an order should be made to add, substitute, remove or correct the name of any party other than a plaintiff (r 3.74(2)). The Court cannot make an order under r 3.74 if prejudice would result that could not be remedied by a costs award, an adjournment or the imposition of terms (r 3.74(3)). The burden is on the party resisting the amendment to show that it would suffer non-compensable prejudice if the amendment is allowed: Castledowns Law Office Management Ltd v FastTrack Technologies Inc, 2012 ABCA 219, at paras 17-18 [Castledowns]. The most common prejudice is the respondent's lost chance to lead more evidence: Balm v 3512061 Canada Ltd, 2003 ABCA 98 at para 73 [Balm]. Other prejudice may exist, including the significant passage of time or the death or incapacitation of a key witness. 25 Exceptions to the general rule allowing for amendments include where the amendment requested is “hopeless”, the amendment seeks to add a new party or a new cause of action after the expiry of a limitation period (unless permitted by statute), and where there is an element of bad faith associated with the failure to plead the amendment in the first instance: Canadian Deposit Insurance Corp v Canadian Commercial Bank, 2000 ABQB 440 at para 11; Foda v Capital Health Region, 2007 ABCA 207 at para 10; CHS v Alberta (Director of Child Welfare), 2006 ABQB 528 at para 11, aff'd 2006 ABCA 355. (B)—Amendments generally 26 The Court has broad discretion to allow amendments, however late or careless, after pleadings have closed: Castledowns at para 16; Brar v Roy, 2005 ABCA 269 at para 17 [Brar]; Balm at para 43; Milfive Investments Ltd v Sefel (1998), 216 AR 196 (Alta CA) at para 3. This generous discretion enables the determination of the real issues between parties, even where the proposed amendment raises a doubtful plea—as long as it is arguable: Balm at para 12; Brar at para 17; Hur v 726913 Alberta Ltd, 2013 ABQB 208 at para 30 [Hur]; Manson Insulation Products Ltd v Crossroads C & I Distributors, 2011 ABQB 51 at paras 43-44. 27 The evidentiary threshold to amend pleadings is low. Only a modest degree of admissible evidence is needed to support any new facts or substance alleged entailing a significant amendment to a pleading before the limitation period has expired; the evidence need not be enough to prove the new allegations on a balance of probabilities: Balm at paras 25-26, 29; Barker at para 12. Even hearsay will suffice: Balm at para 25; Canadian Natural Resources Limited v Arcelormittal Tubular Products Roman SA (Mittal Steel Roman SA), 2012 ABQB 679 at para 50. 28 However, the evidentiary threshold is “significantly elevated” when the proposed amendment alleges fraud, and likely requires evidence which will pass a stiffer test: Balm at para 63; Mikisew Cree First Nation v Canada, 2002 ABCA 110 at para 61 [Mikisew]. In Mikisew, the Court of Appeal explained that there must be good ground, and significant evidence and particulars, to relax the general rule against amending pleadings to allege fraud. Some cases suggest that “exceptional circumstances” are needed. In Condominium Corp. No. 0213028 v. Pasera Corp., 2016 ABQB 477, 2016 CarswellAlta 1645, Justice Strekaf said: 15 The general rule is that pleadings can be amended at any time, however careless or late, subject to four exceptions, as outlined by Chief Justice Wittman in Dow Chemical Canada Inc v Nova Chemicals Corp, 2010 ABQB 524, at paras 20 - 2 [Dow]: Generally, any pleading can be amended no matter how careless or late is the party seeking to amend: Balm v. 3512061 Canada Ltd., 2003 ABCA 98, 327 A.R. 149 at para. 43. This is referred to in Balm as the “classic rule”. The classic rule is subject to four major exceptions: Canadian Deposit Insurance Corp. v. Canadian Commercial Bank, 2000 ABQB 440, 269 A.R. 49 at para. 11; Foda v. Capital Health Region, 2007 ABCA 207 at para. 10; see also C.H.S. v. Alberta (Director of Child Welfare), 2006 ABQB 528, 403 A.R. 103 at para. 11, aff'd 2006 ABCA 355, 401 A.R. 215. Those exceptions are as follows: 1. the amendment would causeserious prejudice to the opposing party, not compensable in costs; 2. the amendment requested is “hopeless” (an amendment that, if were in the original pleadings, would have been struck); 3. unless permitted by statute, the amendment seeks to add a new party or a new cause of action after the expiry of a limitation period; and 4. there is an element of bad faith associated with the failure to plead the amendment in the first instance. Therefore, if no exception applies, the pleadings can generally be amended. … 18 The Court in Dow outlined the options available to the court when an amendment is sought where there are limitations issues (para 64): Traditionally, when there is an issue of limitations and an amendment is sought, a court may: 1. Determine the limitation period has not expired and allow the amendment. 2. Rule the limitation period has expired and therefore consider s. 6 of the Limitations Act which provides for when an amendment can be made beyond the limitation period. 3. Find that because of uncertainty in the evidence, the amendments should be allowed subject to the determination of the limitation issue at trial: Hill v. Hill, [2007] A.J. No. 1515 (Q.B.) at para. 22, aff'd 2007 ABCA 293 at para. 10. A variation of the last option is to determine whether s. 6(2)(b) of the Limitations Act saves a claim otherwise barred by the statute. 2. “Satisfied That The Order Should Be Made” In Kent v. Martin, 2011 ABQB 416, 2011 CarswellAlta 1084, 521 A.R. 313, Justice Tilleman said, at paragraph 9: 9 The requirement in Rule 3.74(2)(b) that the Court must be “satisfied the order should be made” means justice must require the addition of the parties. In the case of a new Defendant, the Court would want to see a link between the new Defendant and the facts and incidents originally alleged against the extant Defendants. There must not be bad faith in the pleadings as against the new Defendant or misconduct by the Plaintiff in bringing them in. Procedurally, the new Defendant should be added as soon as is reasonable in the circumstances; in other words there should not be inexplicable concerns regarding tardiness. Finally, of course, as Rule 3.74(3) states, an order should not be made if prejudice would result that could not be remedied by a costs award, an adjournment or the imposition of terms. 3. General As I read this rule [old Rule 38], the court may add parties if any one of the following situations prevails: (a) If the person ought to have been joined, or (b) If the presence of that person before the court may be necessary in order to enable the court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the cause or matter, or (c) In order to protect the rights or interests of any person or class of persons interested under the plaintiff or defendant. 155569 Canada Ltd. v. 248524 Alberta Ltd. (1988), 93 A.R. 241 at 244 (Q.B.). 4. Purpose of Rule The basic purpose of R. 38 is to prevent any action from being defeated by reason of misjoinder or non-joinder and to allow the necessary amendments in respect of the parties at any stage of the proceedings. The rule is a saving rule and is designed to carry out the intention of the Judicature Act, to secure the determination of all disputes relating to the same subject-matter without a multiplicity of proceeding. Carmacks Construction Ltd. v. Beaumont (Village) (1981), 15 Alta. L.R. (2d) 367 (Master), at 379, per Master Funduk. 5. Test for Misnomer McDonald J., in Bauer v. Alberta (Public Trustee) (1977), 2 Alta. L.R. (2d) 42 (S.C.-T.D.), at 46, approved the test in Davies v. Elsby Bros. Ltd., [1960] 3 All E.R. 672: The test must be: How would a reasonable person receiving the document take it? If, in all the circumstances of the case and looking at the document as a whole, he would say to himself: ‘Of course, it must mean me, but they have got my name wrong’, then there is a case of mere misnomer. If, on the other hand, he would say: ‘I cannot tell from the document itself whether they mean me or not and I shall have to make inquiries’, then it seems to me that one is getting beyond the realm of misnomer. In Osada v. General Hospital (Grey Nuns) of Edmonton (1998), 235 A.R. 31 (Q.B.), the plaintiff applied to substitute as a defendant a Dr. Raymond Muzyka for the originally named Dr. David Muzyka. In allowing the application, Madam Justice Sulyma said, at p. 37: As I have found that this is a case of misnomer, neither the mere passage of time nor expiration of a limitation period is material prejudice for the purpose of this application. Similarly, as I have found a misnomer, there is no requirement that the plaintiff prove a prima facie meritorious issue to be tried as is the case in an application to otherwise amend pleadings. Finally, the plaintiff is required to demonstrate to the court that: (a) he diligently tried to ascertain the identity of Dr. Raymond; and (b) he diligently brought his misnomer application to substitute the name of Dr. Raymond for Dr. David. In Buckler v. Minchau, 2006 ABQB 291, 2006 CarswellAlta 526, 400 A.R. 42, Gallant J. expressed the test for misnomer at p. 53: 52 The test for misnomer has been set out by the Alberta Court of Appeal in Nagy [Nagy v. Phillips (1996), 187 A.R. 97 (Alta. C.A.)]. The Court (at para. 16) adopted the test set out in Davies v. Elsby Brothers Ltd., [1960] 3 All E.R. 672 (C.A.): In Davies, Lord Justice Devlin set out the test for misnomer as follows (at p. 176): … how would a reasonable person receiving the document take it? If, in all the circumstances of the case and looking at the document as a whole, he would say to himself: “Of course it must mean me, but they have got my name wrong,” then there is a case of mere misnomer. If, on the other hand, he would say: “I cannot tell from the document itself whether they mean me or not and I shall have to make inquiries,” then it seems to me that one is getting beyond the realm of misnomer. 53 The Court in Nagy imposed two additional requirements to the misnomer test: (A) Once the Court determines that there has been a misnomer, it must also consider whether the proposed Defendant has been misled or will be substantially injured by the delay in naming him (Nagy at para. 24), and (B) Further, the applicant for an amendment must have been reasonably diligent in seeking to identify the desired defendant and correct the misnomer. See also the annotation “Misnomer” under R. 3.65. 6. Correction of Misnomer … it is wrong to allow the plaintiff to amend ex post facto if it would deprive the defendant of the benefit to which he had become entitled as of right under the statute of limitations. [The amendment is prevented]“… if the amendment involves the addition of a party [defendant] and not the mere correction of misnomer. That principle also applies to the substitution of a party, since substitution involves the addition of a party in replacement of the party that is removed.” The general principle underlying all the cases is that the court should amend, where the opposite party has not been misled, or substantially injured by the error. [These principles]… apply to the question of whether it is a mere misnomer, whether it is the plaintiff or the defendant who is being considered. Bauer v. Alberta (Public Trustee) (1977), 2 Alta. L.R. (2d) 42 at 45, 47 (S.C. T.D.). 7. ‘John Doe’ - what one must do when one determines the identity of ‘John Doe’ In Anglin v. Resler, 2022 ABCA 362, the plaintiff described a defendant as “John Doe” because the actual identity of the defendant was not yet known. The plaintiff later learned the actual identity of “John Doe” and served that person with a copy of the Statement of Claim, and told the person that he was the party named as “John Doe”. The plaintiff did not formally amend the statement of claim to replace “John Doe” with the actual name of the party before noting in default the party described as “John Doe”. The plaintiff subsequently applied to amend both the statement of claim and the noting in default by replacing the name “John Doe” with the actual name of the party. The Court of Appeal held that the amendment to the Statement of Claim should have been promptly made once the actual identity was learned, and that no substantive step should have been taken until that amendment was made. The Court further held that when the application was finally made, it should have been allowed only on condition that the noting in default was set aside. The Court said: [2] The respondent, who was a candidate in an election in 2015, alleges that certain people damaged his election signs during the campaign and conspired to undermine his chances to win the election. When he issued his statement of claim in April 2017 he did not know the names of those persons, so he included as defendants “John Doe” and “Richard Roe”. [3] In February 2018 the respondent came to believe that the appellant Mr. Pankiw was one of those responsible for the alleged damage to his signs. On February 13, 2018, without amending the statement of claim, the respondent served the appellant with the statement of claim, telling the appellant that “you are the John Doe mentioned in it”. [4] As the chambers judge put it: “A standoff then ensued”. The appellant argued that service before amendment of the statement of claim was ineffective. The respondent took the position that he had proper service of the appellant, but took no steps to formally amend the statement of claim to replace the appellant as the named defendant, or to obtain an order declaring service to be good and sufficient. [5] On March 6, 2018 the respondent noted the appellant in default. The Clerk of Court noted in default: “John Doe, identified as Mr. Rick Pankiw in an Affidavit of Service filed February 27, 2018”. No authority or precedent for this procedure has been given. [6] On August 5, 2021 the respondent finally brought an application to amend his statement of claim to name the appellant as a defendant. He also applied to amend the noting in default to specifically name the appellant as the defendant who had been noted in default. . . . . . [8] All parties acknowledge the tradition of naming unknown defendants by using the pseudonyms “John Doe” and “Richard Roe”. However, contrary to the suggestion in paras. 41-43 of the reasons, once the plaintiff finds out the real name of the “John Doe” defendant, it is incumbent on him to take timely steps to amend the pleadings to properly name that defendant. A plaintiff is always required to correctly name every defendant. [9] Any required amendment should be made before any other substantive step is taken in the litigation. In exigent circumstances interlocutory relief (such as an injunction or an Anton Piller order) might be obtained against an unknown John Doe defendant before the style of cause is amended: see MacMillan Bloedel Ltd. v Simpson, 1996 CanLII 165 (SCC), [1996] 2 SCR 1048. However, there is nothing urgent about a noting in default, and in this case the appellant had been identified. Specifically, it would be inappropriate for the plaintiff to attempt to proceed to trial with a known defendant still described as “John Doe”. As the reasons correctly point out at paras. 116-122 the respondent should have moved to amend his pleadings in a timely way. [10] Further, contrary to what is suggested in the reasons at paras. 63-66, the primary obligation is on the plaintiff, not on the unnamed defendant, to move to correct the plaintiff’s pleadings. [11] The reasons suggest at paras. 81-82 that this was a case of misnomer. The use of a pseudonym, however, is not a misnomer. Further, this Court held in Alberta v Railink Ltd, 2003 ABCA 69 at para. 4, 12 Alta LR (4th) 4, 320 AR 373 that in the context of limitations law the law respecting misnomers has been overtaken by s. 6(4) of the Limitations Act, RSA 2000, c. L-12. The present case cannot be distinguished from Railink, and it is unhelpful to analyze the issues here as a misnomer. [12] The Rules of Court variously deal with “adding”, “removing”, “substituting” or “correcting the names of” defendants. The Limitations Act refers to “adding”, “substituting”, or “changing the capacity” of a defendant. It is unnecessary to finally determine into which category replacing a pseudonym with the true name of the defendant would fall. So long as no limitation period is breached, the test generally comes down to whether there is an absence of prejudice that cannot be remedied. . . . . . [16] Nevertheless, delay in bringing an application can be a barrier to relief if prejudice from the delay cannot be remedied by costs or other conditions [….] Rule 3.74(3) bars the substitution of a defendant if prejudice will result. Service before Amendment [17] The respondent served the appellant with the statement of claim before amending the style of cause to correctly name the appellant. The reasons under appeal held at para. 26 that: “No rule requires that a ‘John-Doe-style’ statement of claim be amended before it is served.” It may be literally true that there is no rule that specifically states that the amendment must be made before service, but that is clearly the presumptive rule. The service in this case can, at best, be described as irregular. At the least, it was incumbent on the respondent to immediately amend the statement of claim after the purported service, advise the appellant that that had been done, and seek an order under R. 11.27 validating service. [18] The question then is whether the respondent’s failure to do so in this case was a fatal error. The appellant was given a copy of the statement of claim, and told that he was the “John Doe” named in it. That had the effect, at least, of fulfilling one of the functional purposes of service, namely to put him on notice that his legal rights had been engaged: Sandhu v MEG Place LP Investment Corp, 2012 ABCA 266 at paras. 18-19, 542 AR 12. While it was problematic for the chambers judge to declare that valid service had been effected on February 13, 2018, that does not have an impact on the outcome of this appeal. [19] Rule 3.76 provides that when a defendant is added or substituted, that defendant must be served and has the same right to file a defence as a defendant that was originally named:

Misnomer and Limitations Misnomer is often said to be an exception to the general rule barring addition or substitution of parties after the limitation period has expired. Strictly speaking, it is no exception at all. Where there is a true misnomer, the party is the same all along, and need not be changed. … An example or two will help. Suppose that just before the limitation period expires, a client instructs his lawyer to start a suit. Everyone calls the client “Jim Smith”, and the lawyer assumes that “Jim” is a nickname for James. So he sues in the name of James Smith. In fact, “Jim” is short for Jimson. So far as the lawyer and his client are concerned, there is no error as to persons at all, merely an error as to description. To correct it is not really to change parties. …. Counsel for the respondent also points out to us that the existence of a separate person or company with the name given is not necessarily a bar to finding misnomer. … I agree with that proposition. If James had not been involved in any of the matters sued over, and no one connected thought he had, and indeed the lawyers and the defendants had never heard of him, he would be irrelevant. [22] Because there was no effective service in February 2018, the respondent was not in a position to note the appellant in default.
Further, noting a John Doe defendant in default when the actual identity of that defendant is known is not authorized by the Rules.

[23] This case should be contrasted with those rare situations where a) an unknown defendant is named as John Doe, b) an order authorizing or validating substitutional or other service is obtained, c) the Court is satisfied that effective personal service was achieved by the authorized means on the John Doe defendant even though its identity remains unknown, and d) that John Doe defendant continues to conceal its identity and refuses to engage with the litigation: see for example McGee v Samra, 2021 ONSC 2540.
However, once the John Doe defendant is identified, amendments to the pleadings are required.
[24] A plaintiff who notes a defendant in default must diligently comply with the applicable rules.
As held in Kraushar v Kraushar, 2019 ABCA 186 at para.
5, 88 Alta LR (6th) 69: Where there is a non-trivial flaw in the process leading up to the default judgment, the defendant, acting promptly, has a right to have it set aside: . . .

In the face of an active bona fide dispute between the parties over the validity of the pleadings, and the validity of service, it was inappropriate for the respondent to note the appellant in default before making the necessary amendments: Anstar Enterprises Ltd v Transamerica Life Canada, 2009 ABCA 196 at paras.
As the chambers judge held at para.
121 the path taken by the respondent was a “path that no reasonable litigant should take again”.
This irregularity would justify setting aside the noting in default.
The requested amendment should only have been granted if the prejudice arising from these irregular procedures was reversed.
Conclusion [25] In summary, an application to amend can be granted on conditions that are designed to eliminate any prejudice that has been occasioned.
In this case, the application to amend should only have been granted on the condition that the noting in default be set aside.
[26] The appeal is allowed in part.
The order permitting the amendment to the statement of claim is confirmed, but only on the condition that the noting in default is set aside.
The appellant must file his defence within 20 days.
Misnomer and Limitations Misnomer is often said to be an exception to the general rule barring addition or substitution of parties after the limitation period has expired.
Strictly speaking, it is no exception at all.
Where there is a true misnomer, the party is the same all along, and need not be changed. … An example or two will help.
Suppose that just before the limitation period expires, a client instructs his lawyer to start a suit.
Everyone calls the client “Jim Smith”, and the lawyer assumes that “Jim” is a nickname for James.
So he sues in the name of James Smith.
In fact, “Jim” is short for Jimson.
So far as the lawyer and his client are concerned, there is no error as to persons at all, merely an error as to description.
To correct it is not really to change parties. ….
Counsel for the respondent also points out to us that the existence of a separate person or company with the name given is not necessarily a bar to finding misnomer. … I agree with that proposition.
In the example above, the client Jimson Smith might happen to have a brother or cousin named James Smith.
If James had not been involved in any of the matters sued over, and no one connected thought he had, and indeed the lawyers and the defendants had never heard of him, he would be irrelevant.
His existence would not bar finding a misnomer.
Therefore it follows that where misnomer is suggested, it is important to characterize the error.
In any event, to characterize the error as seen by the relevant person.
Was the wrong entity put into the pleading?
If so, and if a lawyer drafted the pleading, the wrong entity would be put there because that entity was believed to be the one injured (as described in the pleading).
Lawyers know that only the person wronged can sue.
For example, the information may have passed through several hands, and the lawyer may have been misinformed as to who was injured and taken to the hospital.
Or misinformed as to which of several cargo shipments was damaged by the sea.
In such a case, one must truly change the party to correct the error.
As said in Yancey v.
Neis, [(1999), 73 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 239 (C.A.)]… that is “a deliberate but misinformed decision to omit the” party in question.
But if everyone knows who suffered the loss, and there is an explanation for how his or her name came to be inaccurately recited, or that is obvious, then the error may be misnomer.
Rocklake Enterprises Ltd. v.
Timberjack Inc.
L.R.
(3d) 257 (C.A.) at 266-267, per Côté J.A.

Interest in Action On the wider construction of the rule, I do not understand where the line is to be drawn—it is conceded that it must be drawn somewhere—between a commercial interest in the question involved in the case and a legal one.
It is not enough that the intervener should be commercially or indirectly interested in the answer to the question: he must be directly or legally interested in the answer.
A person is legally interested in the answer only if he can say that it may lead to a result that will affect him legally—that is by curtailing his legal rights.
That will not be the case unless an order may be made in the action which will operate on something in which he is legally interested.
Nowek v.
Lubeck (1984), 54 A.R.
91 (Q.B.), at 92, citing Devlin J. in Amon v.
Raphael Tuck & Sons Ltd.[1956] 1 All E.R.
In Anderson Exploration Ltd. v.
Pan-Alberta Gas Ltd.
109 (Q.B.), Moore C.J.Q.B. had before him an application to add two new defendants to an action.
With respect to the test to be applied, he said, at pp.
110-11: In Bernhart v.
Umisk Farms Ltd.

Master), Master Funduk succinctly states the two-part test that must be satisfied before amendments will be allowed: 1) Is it appropriate to deal with the claims that the plaintiffs are advancing in the existing action?
2) Will the proposed defendants be prejudiced if the amendments are granted?

sentences.text: Adding, removing or substituting parties to originating application

paragraphs.text: (1) In an action started by originating application no party or person may be added or substituted as a party to the action except in accordance with this rule. (2) On application of a party or person, the Court may order that a person be added or substituted as a party to the action, (a) in the case of a person to be added or substituted as an originating applicant, if consent of the person proposed to be added or substituted is filed with the application; (b) in the case of an application to add or substitute a person as a respondent, or to remove or correct the name of a party, if the Court is satisfied the order should be made. (3) The Court may not make an order under this rule if prejudice would result for a party that could not be remedied by a costs award, an adjournment or the imposition of terms.
